questions.subject: Polity
question: Consider the following statements regarding Morley-Minto Reforms:
Statement-I:
Elected members of Imperial Legislative Council were elected indirectly by the provincial council.
Statement-II:
It introduced separate electorate for Muslims and depressed classes.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

options.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
options.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
options.C: Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
options.D: Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct

solution: Correct Option: (c)
Explanation:
Statement II is incorrect: It introduced a separate electorate for Muslims only.
Supplementary notes:
Morley-Minto Reforms/Indian Councils Act of 1909
The British Government played the game of Divide and Rule' and tried to win over moderate nationalist opinion so that the militant nationalists could be isolated and suppressed.
To placate the moderate nationalists it announced constitutional concessions through the Indian Councils Act of 1909 which are known as the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909.
Features of the act are:
It increased the number of elected members in the Imperial Legislative Council and the provincial councils.

But most of the elected members were elected indirectly, by the provincial council in the case of the Imperial Council and by municipal committees and district boards in the case of provincial councils.
Some of the elected seats were reserved for landlords and British capitalists in India.

The reformed councils still enjoyed no real power, being merely advisory bodies. The reforms in no way changed the undemocratic and foreign character of British rule or the fact of foreign economic exploitation of the country.

The Reforms also introduced the system of separate electorates under which all Muslims were grouped in separate constituencies from which Muslims alone could be elected. This was done in the name of protecting the Muslim minority. But in reality, this was a part of the policy of dividing Hindus and Muslims and thus maintaining British supremacy in India.

The moderate nationalists did not fully support the Morley-Minto Reforms. They soon realized that the Reforms had not really granted much. But they decided to cooperate with the Government in working the reforms.
L2: Approachable

questions.subject: Polity
question: Consider the following statements:
1. It accepted the demand of Pakistan.
2. It provided for three-tier government at union and two tier at provincial level.
3. Provinces were to have full autonomy and residual powers.
How many of the above statements is/are correct regarding recommendations of Cabinet Mission Plan?
solution: Correct Option: (a)
Explanation:
Statement 1 is incorrect: The plan rejected the demand for a full-fledged Pakistan
Statement 2 is incorrect: Three-tier executive and legislature at all i.e. provincial, section and union levels.
Supplementary notes:
Cabinet Mission Plan
The Cabinet Mission reached Delhi on March 24, 1946. It had prolonged discussions with Indian leaders of all parties and groups on the issues of:
Interim government; and
Principles and procedures for framing a new constitution giving freedom to India.
The plan rejected the demand for a full-fledged Pakistan, because:
Pakistan so formed would include a large non-Muslim population-38% in the North-West and 48% in the North-East;

The very principle of communal self-determination would claim separation of Hindu-majority western Bengal and Sikh-and Hindu-dominated Ambala and Jullundur divisions of Punjab (already some Sikh leaders were demanding a separate state if the country was partitioned);
Deep-seated regional ties would be disturbed if Bengal and Punjab were partitioned;
Partition would entail economic and administrative problems, for instance, the problem of communication between the western and eastern parts of Pakistan; and
The division of the armed forces would be dangerous.
Three-tier executive and legislature at provincial, section and union levels.
Other recommendations of Cabinet Mission Plan:
Grouping of existing provincial assemblies into three sections:
Section-A: Madras, Bombay, Central Provinces, United Provinces, Bihar and Orissa (Hindu-majority provinces).
Section-B: Punjab, North-West Frontier Province and Sindh (Muslim- majority provinces).
Section-C: Bengal and Assam (Muslim-majority provinces).
A common centre would control defence, communication and external affairs.
Provinces were to have full autonomy and residual powers.

After the first general elections, a province was to be free to come out of a group and after 10 years, a province was to be free to call for a reconsideration of the group or the Union constitution. Meanwhile, an interim government to be formed from the constituent assembly.
L2: Approachable

questions.subject: Polity
question: How many of the following statements about Delhi Proposals is/are incorrect?
1. It consisted the demands of Muslim League that was to be incorporated into the draft constitution.
2. It provisioned for joint electorates in place of separate electorates.
3. It demanded one-third representation to Muslims in Central Legislative Assembly.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
solution: Correct Option: (d)
Explanation:
All statement are correct.
Supplementary notes:
Delhi Proposals

In December 1927, a large number of Muslim leaders had met at Delhi at the Muslim League session and evolved four proposals for their demands to be incorporated into the draft constitution. This was called as 'Delhi Proposals'.
Following were the 4 points of proposal:
Joint electorates in place of separate electorates with reserved seats for Muslims;
One-third representation to Muslims in Central Legislative Assembly;
Representation to Muslims in Punjab and Bengal in proportion to their population; and
Formation of three new Muslim majority provinces Sindh, Baluchistan and North-West Frontier Province.

questions.subject: Polity
question: Consider the following statements regarding Government of India Act, 1935:
1. It established an All India Federation comprising British Provinces and princely states.
2. It abolished dyarchy at the Provincial level and introduced it at the Centre.
3. It extended the principle of communal representation by providing separate electorates for depressed classes, women and labour.
How many of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution: Correct Option: (d)
Explanation:
All statements are correct.
Supplementary notes:
Salient Features of Government of India Act 1935

All India Federation: The Act provided for an All-India Federation comprising the British Indian Provinces and the princely states. The terms on which a state could join the federation were mentioned in the Instrument of Accession.

Provincial Autonomy: One redeeming feature of the new Act was that it marked the beginning of the Provincial Autonomy. It was definitely an advance on the Act of 1919. Moreover, the Act introduced responsible governments in provinces, that is, the governor was required to act with the advice of ministers responsible to the provincial legislature. This came into effect in 1937 and was discontinued in 1939.

Division of Subjects: The approach to form the federation and implement provincial autonomy paved the way for the division of subjects between the Centre and the Provinces. The division of subjects that were given by the Government of India Act, 1919 was revised and added some more subjects in it by this Act of 1935 and included three lists.

Dyarchy at the Centre: The Act of 1935 abolished dyarchy at the Provincial level and introduced it at the Centre. There were two categories of federal subjects, Reserved subjects and Transferred subjects.

Bicameral legislature: Under the Government of India Act, 1935, the Central Legislature was bicameral, consisting of Federal Assembly and Council of States. The Council of States was to be upper house and a permanent body with one third of its membership retiring every 3rd year.. The Federal Assembly was the lower house with the tenure of five years.

Retention of Communal Electorate: It further extended the principle of communal representation by providing separate electorates for depressed classes (scheduled castes), women and labour (workers). The Muslims got 33 1/3 percent of the seats in the Federal Legislature although their number was much less than one-third of the total population of British India.

Abolition of India Council: The new Act abolished India Council and provided for the appointment by the Secretary of State and his team of Advisers whose number was not to be less than 3 and not more than 65.
Federal Court: The Government of India Act, 1935 provided for the establishment of a Federal Court which would interpret the Act and adjudicate disputes relating to the federal matters.
L3: Real Challenge

question: Which of the following were the recommendations of the Simon Commission?
1. Continuation of Dyarchy introduced by Government of India Act 1919.
2. Dominion status for Burma
3. Special power for the protection of minorities comes under the Governor
4. Extension of responsible government in provinces
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
solution: Correct Option: (b)
Explanation:
Option (b) is correct.
Supplementary notes:
Simon Commission
The Government of India Act 1919 made a provision for a review committee on its working after 10 years.
However the conservative government was staring at defeat and it felt that this constitutional question couldn't be left in the hands of inexperienced labor party.
Thus the Indian statutory commission popularly known as the Simon commission was appointed in 1927. A commission established by Baldwin to inquire into political conditions in British India.

It consisted of seven members, and was chaired jointly by John Simon and Clement Attlee. It met a hostile reception in India, and was boycotted there because it had no Indian members. The recommendations were -
Continuation of communal representation,
Abolition of diarchy,
Extension of responsible government in provinces,
Creation of Indian federation of British India and princely states,
Dominion status for Burma and should be provided its own Constitution and
Special power for the safeguarding of province and the protection of minorities comes under the Governor powers.

questions.subject: Polity
question: Which of the following demands were parts of the Jinnah's fourteen points raised in 1929?
1. 50% Muslim representation in the central legislature
2. Separation of Sindh from Bombay
3. Constitutional reforms in Punjab and Bengal
4. Full religious freedom to all communities
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
solution: Correct Option: (c)
Explanation:
Statement 1 is incorrect: Since Jinnah demanded one-third Muslim representation in central legislature
Statement 3 is incorrect: He demanded constitutional reforms in NWFP and Baluchistan.
Supplementary notes:
Jinnah fourteen point

The Fourteen Points of Jinnah were proposed by Muhammad Ali Jinnah. Jinnah's aim was to get more rights for Muslims. The report was given in a meeting of the council of the All-India Muslim League on 9 March 1929. His 14 points are as follow
The form of the future constitution should be federal, with the residuary powers vested in the provinces:
A uniform measure of autonomy shall be guaranteed to all provinces;

All legislatures in the country and other elected bodies shall be constituted on the definite principle of adequate and effective representation of minorities in every province without reducing the majority in any province to a minority or even equality;
In the Central Legislature, Muslim representation shall not be less than one third;

Representation of communal groups shall continue to be by means of separate electorate as at present: provided it shall be open to any community, at any time to abandon its separate electorate in favour of a joint electorate.
Any territorial distribution that might at any time be necessary shall not in any way affect the Muslim majority.
Full religious liberty, i.e., liberty of belief, worship and observance, propaganda, association and education, shall be guaranteed to all communities.

No bill or resolution or any part thereof shall be passed in any legislature or any other elected body if three fourths of the members of any community in that particular body oppose it as being injurious to the interests of that community or in the alternative, such other method is devised as may be found feasible and practicable to deal with such cases.
Sindh should be separated from the Bombay Presidency.
Reforms should be introduced in the North West Frontier Province and Baluchistan on the same footing as in the other provinces.

Provision should be made in the constitution giving Muslims an adequate share, along with the other Indians, in all the services of the state and in local self-governing bodies having due regard to the requirements of efficiency.

The constitution should embody adequate safeguards for the protection of Muslim culture and for the protection and promotion of Muslim education, language, religion, personal laws and Muslim charitable institutions and for their due share in the grants-in-aid given by the state and by local self-governing bodies.
No cabinet, either central or provincial, should be formed without there being a proportion of at least one-third Muslim ministers.
No change shall be made in the constitution by the Central Legislature except with the concurrence of the States constituting of the Indian Federation.
L3: Real Challenge

questions.subject: Polity
question: Consider the following statements regarding August declaration of 1917:
1. It talked about limited self-government, a first such British proposal in a non-white colony.
2. It was unanimously welcomed by both moderates and extremist.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution: Correct Option: (a)
Explanation:
Statement 2 is incorrect: August declaration was not welcomed by extremist faction of INC.
Supplementary notes:
August declaration of 1917

Edwin Samuel Montagu who was Secretary of State for India (1917-1922), made a declaration in August 1917 which defined the aim of Policies of British Empire in India. This declaration is also called August Declaration or Montague's Statement.
Montague statement was the precursor to the Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms).
Provisions of the Montague Statement
The increasing involvement of Indians in every branch of administration.
Montague statement proposed for gradual development of Self-governing institution considering the progressive realisation of responsible government in India.

The sole authority to judge the time and measure of each advancement towards self-government would be British Government and Government of India and in this, they would be guided by the responsible Indian leaders.
The declaration focussed on limited self-government at first, it was the first such British proposal in a non-white colony for any form of representative government.

Moderate leaders welcomed the Montague's statement while Extremist leaders objected to it as no specific time frame was given and the Government alone was to decide the nature and the timing of advance towards a responsible government.
L2: Approachable

questions.subject: Polity
question: Consider the following statements regarding Shimla Conference/Wavell Plan:
1. The commander-in-chief in the executive council should be an Indian.
2. Muslims and Hindus were to have equal representation.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution: Correct Option: (b)
Explanation:
Statement 1 is incorrect: With the exception of the governor-general and the commander-in-chief, all members of the executive council were to be Indians.
Supplementary notes:
Shimla Conference/Wavell Plan

At the end of the Second World War at the initiative of Viceroy Lord Wavell, the Congress leaders were released from Jail in mid-June in 1945 and invited to Shimla to work out an interim political agreement under which Indians would be responsible for running the country.
The main proposals under Shimla Conference/Wavell Plan were:
With the exception of the governor-general and the commander-in-chief, all members of the executive council were to be Indians.
Hindus and Muslims were to have equal representation.
The reconstructed council was to function as an interim government within the framework of the 1935 Act (i.e. not responsible to the Central Assembly).
Governor General was to exercise his veto on the advice of ministers.
Representatives of different parties were, to submit a joint list to the viceroy for nominations to the executive council. If a joint list was not possible, then separate lists were to be submitted.
Possibilities were to be, kept open for negotiations on a new constitution once the war was finally won.
L1: Elementary

questions.subject: Polity
question: Consider the following statements regarding the Nehru Report:
1. Muslim League rejected the Nehru Report primarily because of the absence of separate electorates for Muslims.
2. The younger section of congress led by Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhash Bose supported the Nehru Report on the idea of Purna Swaraj.
3. Independence for India League was formed by Motilal Nehru, the Chairman of the Committee that drafted the Report, when it was rejected by the Congress.
How many of the above statements is/are correct?
solution: Correct Option: (a)
Explanation:
Statement 2 is incorrect: The younger section rejected the Nehru Report on the idea of dominion status.
Statement 3 is incorrect: Nehru and Subhash Bose rejected the Congress'modified goal and jointly set up the Independence for India League. Instead, the Nehru Report was accepted by the Congress.
Supplementary notes:
Nehru Report

The All-Parties Conference, in February 1928, included the Congress representatives, All-India Liberal Federation, All India Muslim League, Sikh Central League, Hindu Mahasabha and others. This Conference was presided over by Dr. M.A. Ansari. It was agreed that in framing the Constitution of India, the principle of full Dominion responsible self-government should be kept in mind. After two subsequent meetings of All-Parties, in Bombay and in Lucknow, the Constitution was ratified. It asked for full Dominion Status and had provisions for having responsible governments at Centre as well as in the Provinces.

The Conference, on 19 May 1928, constituted a committee to draft the Constitution. Some of the notable members of this Committee were: Motilal Nehru (Chairman), Sir Ali Imam, Tej Bahadur Sapru and Subash Chandra Bose. M.R. Jayakar and Annie Besant joined the Committee later.
Jawaharlal Nehru was appointed the secretary to the Committee.
Reactions to Nehru Report

The Nehru Report received a mixed response from Indians. The Hindustan Times, in an editorial, argued that the report marked ... the final death of communal egotism and the birth of a national consciousness in the country...'. The editorial also stated that Lord Birkenhead's challenge was met and that ...we have drawn the Magna Carta of our liberty'.

However, the political consensus around the report broke down: the Muslim League, which was part of the All-Parties Conference, rejected the Report primarily because of the absence of separate electorates for Muslims. The dropping of the separate electorates was a reversal of the agreement between the Congress and the League that was encoded in the Congress-League Pact, 1916 (the Lucknow Pact). The Hindu Mahasabha opposed the formation of the new provinces and the communal representation in Bengal and Punjab. They pressed for a strictly unitary system.

Not only were the Muslim League, the Hindu Mahasabha and the Sikh communalists unhappy about the Nehru Report, but the younger section of the Congress led by Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhash Bose were also angered. The younger section regarded the idea of dominion status in the report as a step backward, and the developments at the All-Parties Conference strengthened their criticism of the dominion status idea.
Nehru and Subhash Bose rejected the Congress' modified goal and jointly set up the Independence for India League.
L3: Real Challenge

questions.subject: Polity
question: With reference to creation of states on linguistic basis in India, consider the following pairs?
Commissions | Aim
1. S.K. Dhar | Reorganization on administrative convenience
2. JVP Commission | Reorganization on language convenience
3. Fazl Ali Commission | one language-one state
Which of the above pairs is/are correct?
solution: Correct Option: (c)
Explanation

Pair 1 is correctly matched: Also known as the first Linguistic Provinces Commission of independent India, it was set up under the chairmanship of S. K. Dhar, a retired judge of the Allahabad High Court. The commission submitted its report in December 1948 and recommended the reorganization of states on the basis of administrative convenience rather than linguistic factor. Commission argued that the country was not yet free from the dangers of external aggression (The Kashmir war had just concluded in a ceasefire) and the Indian states have not been properly integrated. It said that the country could not bear the financial and administrative strain of creating new provinces at the time of its economic crisis situation after Independence

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched: The rise of resentment among the people led to the appointment of another Linguistic Provinces Committee by the Indian National Congress in December 1948. The members of the committee were Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya. Hence it was popularly known as JVP Committee. The committee in its April 1949 final report also rejected the language as the basis for a reorganization of Indian states.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched: The commission broadly accepted language as the basis of the reorganization of states, however, it rejected the theory of one language one state'. It suggested to include the following four factors before making any plans for state reorganization:
Unity and Security of the country must be preserved.
Cultural and Linguistic homogeneity to be promoted.
Financial, economic and administrative aspects must be considered.
Planning must be done by keeping in the forefront the welfare of the people in each state as well as of the nation as a whole.
L3: Real Challenge

questions.subject: Polity
question: Consider the following statements regarding the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms:
Statement-I:
Reserved subjects were under the direct control of the British-appointed Governor.
Statement-II:
While transferred subjects were under the control of ministers responsible to the provincial legislatures.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

options.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
options.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
options.C: Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
options.D: Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct

solution: Correct Option: (b)
Explanation:
Both statements are correct.
Supplementary notes:
Government of India Act, 1919

The Government of India Act, 1919, also known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms, was a significant piece of legislation during the British colonial rule in India. It introduced a series of constitutional reforms and changes in the governance of India. The core subjects of the Government of India Act, 1919, included:

Diarchy in Provincial Governments: The Act introduced the concept of diarchy in the provinces of British India. This meant that certain subjects were divided into two categories: reserved and transferred. Reserved subjects were under the direct control of the British-appointed Governor, while transferred subjects were under the control of ministers responsible to the provincial legislatures. This introduced a limited form of responsible government at the provincial level.

Legislative Councils: The Act expanded the role of legislative councils in both the provinces and at the central level. It increased the size and introduced a limited form of direct elections in the provincial legislative councils. The central legislative council was also expanded to include more elected members.

Separate Electorates: The Act continued the provision of separate electorates for religious minorities, ensuring that Muslims, Sikhs, and other communities had reserved seats in legislative councils. This was a policy aimed at recognizing and protecting the interests of various religious communities.

Franchise: The Act extended the franchise, allowing a larger section of the population to vote and participate in the electoral process. However, the right to vote was still limited, and the majority of the population remained disenfranchised.

Public Service: The Act made provisions for the protection of the interests of civil servants. It also established a Public Service Commission to oversee the recruitment and functioning of public servants.
Finance: The Act made provisions for a system of dual control over finances, with the Indian legislature having some authority over taxation and expenditure.
Sedition Laws: The Act introduced sedition laws that gave the government extensive powers to suppress political dissent and freedom of speech.
Bicameral Federal Legislature: At the central level, it introduced a federal system with a bicameral legislature, consisting of the Council of States and the Legislative Assembly.

The Government of India Act, 1919, was a significant step toward the gradual devolution of power to Indians and paved the way for further constitutional reforms in subsequent years. It also marked a shift from authoritarian rule to a more inclusive and representative form of governance, albeit with many limitations and safeguards in place to protect British interests.
L2: Approachable

questions.subject: Polity
question: Consider the following statements regarding the Simon Commission's recommendations and their impact on India's freedom struggle:
1. Under the Indian Constitutional Reform, there were absences of any Indian members.
2. The Simon Commission recommended maintaining the status quo.
3. As a result, the Indian National Congress raised the demand for Swaraj.
4. The Simon Commission indirectly contributed to the eventual passage of the Government of India Act, 1935.
How many of the above statements is/are incorrect?
solution: Correct Option: (d)
Explanation:
All statement are correct:
Supplementary notes:
Simon Commission

The Simon Commission, formally known as the Statutory Commission on Indian Constitutional Reform, was a British parliamentary commission established in 1927 to review and make recommendations for constitutional reforms in India.

The commission was headed by Sir John Simon, a British politician, and it consisted entirely of British members, with no Indian representation. This lack of Indian representation led to widespread protests and opposition in India.
Recommendations of the Simon Commission:

No Indian Representation: The most contentious aspect of the Simon Commission was the absence of any Indian members. This decision was viewed as undemocratic and insensitive to Indian aspirations for self-governance.

Status Quo: The Simon Commission recommended maintaining the status quo, suggesting that no immediate constitutional reforms were necessary. This was seen as a betrayal of Indian expectations for self-rule and constitutional changes.
Impact:

Protests and Boycott: The Simon Commission's all-British composition triggered widespread protests and boycotts in India. Indians viewed it as an insult to their demands for self-governance and felt that the British government was not genuinely interested in addressing their concerns.

Lack of Credibility: The Simon Commission lost credibility in the eyes of the Indian population due to its composition and recommendations. Indians saw it as an attempt by the British to maintain control over India without granting meaningful reforms.

Demand for Swaraj: The Simon Commission and the ensuing protests further fueled the demand for Swaraj, or self-rule, among Indians. The Indian National Congress, under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru, began advocating for complete independence as the only acceptable solution.

Round Table Conferences: In response to the growing unrest in India, the British government organized a series of Round Table Conferences in London between 1930 and 1932. These conferences aimed to discuss constitutional reforms and included Indian representation. While they failed to produce a consensus on a new constitution, they marked a shift toward more inclusive discussions.

Government of India Act, 1935: The Simon Commission indirectly contributed to the eventual passage of the Government of India Act, 1935. This act introduced significant constitutional reforms, including the establishment of provincial autonomy and federal structure, which became the basis for India's governance until independence in 1947.
L4: Incapacitated

questions.subject: Polity
question: Consider the following statements regarding Charter Act of 1813:
1. All trade with India was open to all British subjects.
2. After this act, the company continued to appoint officials in India.
3. The debts of the company were taken over by the Government of India.
How many of the above statements is/are correct?
solution: Correct Option: (a)
Explanation:
Statement 1 is incorrect: Trade in tea and trade with China was still exclusive to the Company.
Statement 3 is incorrect: The debts of the company were taken over by the Government of India after the Charter Act of 1833.
Supplementary notes:
Charter Act of 1813

By the Charter Act of 1813, the trade monopoly of the Company in India was ended and trade with India was thrown open to all British subjects. But trade in tea and trade with China was still exclusive to the Company.
The Government and the revenues of India continued to be in the hands of the Company. The Company also continued to appoint its officials in India.
L2: Approachable

questions.subject: Polity
question: With reference to the Indian Councils Act of 1861, consider the following statements:
1. Members could only discuss actions of the administration.
2. Viceroy could disallow any of the acts made by the Legislative council.
3. Indian nationalist opinion was represented in the council.
How many of the above statements is/are incorrect?
solution: Correct Option: (d)
Explanation:

Statement 1 is incorrect: It could not discuss the actions of the administration. But, the members were allowed to ask questions in the Council but not allowed to ask supplementaries or discuss the answer.
Statement 2 is incorrect: Secretary of State could disallow any of Legislative council Acts.
Statement 3 is incorrect: Indian nationalist opinion was not represented in the imperial legislative council. But, the non-official Indian members were added to the Council to represent Indian views.
Supplementary notes:
Imperial Legislative Council
The Indian Councils Act of 1861 enlarged the Governor-General Council for the purpose of making laws in which capacity it was known as, the Imperial Legislative Council.

The Imperial Legislative Council possessed no real powers and should not be seen as a sort of elementary or weak parliament was merely an advisory body. It could not discuss any important measure and no financial measures at all, without the previous approval of the government. It had no control over the budget.
It could not discuss the actions of the administration; the members could not even ask a question about them.
In other words, the Legislative Council had no control over the executive. Secretary of State could disallow any of its Acts.
Thus, the only function of the Legislative Council was to ditto official measures and give them the appearance of having been passed by a legislative body.
The non-official Indian members were added to the Council to represent Indian views.

The Indian members of the legislative Council were few in number and were not elected by the Indian people but were nominated by the Governor-General whose choice invariably fell on princes and their ministers, big zamindars, big merchants, or retired senior government officials.
They were thoroughly unrepresentative of the Indian people or of the growing nationalist opinion.
L3: Real Challenge

questions.subject: Polity
question: Which of the following was not a salient feature of the Regulating Act of 1773?

options.A: Creation of Executive Council for the Governor-General of Bengal
options.B: Prohibited servants of the company to engage in private trade
options.C: Court of directors were required to report on revenue affairs in India
options.D: Restoring legislative powers of Bombay and Madras Presidencies

solution: Correct Option: (d)
Explanation:
Option (d) is correct
Supplementary notes:
Salient Features of Regulating Act of 1773
The Regulating Act of 1773 permitted the Company to retain its former possessions and power in Indian but the management was brought under control by the British Government.
It designated the Governor of Bengal as the 'Governor-General of Bengal and created an Executive Council of four members to assist him. The first such Governor-General was Lord Warren Hastings.
It made the governors of Bombay and Madras presidencies subordinate to the governor-general of Bengal, unlike earlier, when the three presidencies were independent of one another.
It provided for the establishment of a Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774) comprising one chief justice and three other judges.
It prohibited the servants of the Company from engaging in any private trade or accepting presents or bribes from the 'natives'.

It strengthened the control of the British Government over the Company by requiring the Court of Directors (governing body of the Company) to report on its revenue, civil, and military affairs in India.
L1: Elementary

questions.subject: Polity
question: How many of the following changes was/were introduced by the Charter Act of 1853?
1. It abolished the system of patronage and introduced the system of open competition as a method of recruitment in civil service.
2. It introduced for the first time local representation in the Indian (Central) Legislative Council.
3. It separated, for the first time, the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's Council.
How many of the above statements is/are correct?
solution: Correct Option: (a)
Explanation
All statements are correct
Supplementary notes:
The Charter Act of 1853
It separated, for the first time, the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's council. It provided for addition of six new members called legislative councillors to the council.

In other words, it established a separate Governor-General's legislative council which came to be known as the Indian (Central) Legislative Council. This legislative wing of the council functioned as a mini-Parliament, adopting the same procedures as the British Parliament.
Thus, legislation, for the first time, was treated as a special function of the government, requiring special machinery and special process.

It introduced an open competition system of selection and recruitment of civil servants. The covenanted civil service was, thus, thrown open to the Indians also. Accordingly, the Macaulay Committee (the Committee on the Indian Civil Service) was appointed in 1854.

It extended the Company's rule and allowed it to retain the possession of Indian territories on trust for the British Crown. But, it did not specify any particular period, unlike the previous Charters. This was a clear indication that the Company's rule could be terminated at any time the Parliament liked.

It introduced, for the first time, local representation in the Indian (Central) Legislative Council. Of the six new legislative members of the Governor-General's council, four members were appointed by the local (provincial) governments of Madras, Bombay, Bengal and Agra.
L3: Real Challenge

Supplementary notes
Charter Act of 1813

By the Charter Act of 1813, the trade monopoly of the Company in India was ended and trade with India was thrown open to all British subjects. But trade in tea and trade with China was still exclusive to the Company.
The Government and the revenues of India continued to be in the hands of the Company.
The Company also continued to appoint its officials in India.

questions.subject: Polity
question: 23. Consider the following statements regarding the Imperial Legislative Council:
1. Members could discuss actions of the administration.
2. Viceroy could disallow any of the acts made by the Legislative council.
3. Indian nationalist opinion was also represented in the council.
How many of the above statements is/are incorrect?
solution: Statement 1 is incorrect: It could not discuss the actions of the administration.
Statement 2 is incorrect: Secretary of State could disallow any of Legislative council Acts.
Statement 3 is incorrect: Indian nationalist opinion was not represented in the imperial legislative council.
Supplementary notes
Imperial Legislative Council
The Indian Councils Act of 1861 enlarged the Governor-General Council for the purpose of making laws in which capacity it was known as, the Imperial Legislative Council.

The Imperial Legislative Council possessed no real powers and should not be seen as a sort of elementary or weak parliament was merely an advisory body. It could not discuss any important measure and no financial measures at all, without the previous approval of the government. It had no control over the budget.
It could not discuss the actions of the administration; the members could not even ask a question about them.
In other words, the Legislative Council had no control over the executive.

Secretary of State could disallow any of its Acts. Thus, the only function of the Legislative Council was to ditto official measures and give them the appearance of having been passed by a legislative body.

The non-official Indian members were added to the Council to represent Indian views. The Indian members of the legislative Council were few in number and were not elected by the Indian people but were nominated by the Governor-General whose choice invariably fell on princes and their ministers, big zamindars, big merchants, or retired senior government officials.
They were thoroughly unrepresentative of the Indian people or of the growing nationalist opinion.

questions.subject: Polity
question: 29. Consider the following statements regarding Government of India Act, 1935:
1. It established an All-India Federation comprising British Provinces and princely states.
2. It abolished dyarchy at the Provincial level and introduced it at the Centre.
3. Separate electorates were provided for Muslims, Sikhs and others, but not to Depressed Classes.
How many of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution: All statements are correct
Supplementary notes
Salient Features of Government of India Act 1935

All India Federation: The Act provided for an All-India Federation comprising the British Indian Provinces and the princely states. The terms on which a state could join the federation were mentioned in the Instrument of Accession.

Provincial Autonomy: One redeeming feature of the new Act was that it marked the beginning of the Provincial Autonomy. It was definitely an advance on the Act of 1919. Moreover, the Act introduced responsible governments in provinces, that is, the governor was required to act with the advice of ministers responsible to the provincial legislature. This came into effect in 1937 and was discontinued in 1939.

Division of Subjects: The approach to form the federation and implement provincial autonomy paved the way for the division of subjects between the Centre and the Provinces. The division of subjects that were given by the Government of India Act, 1919 was revised and added some more subjects in it by this Act of 1935 and included three lists.

Dyarchy at the Centre: The Act of 1935 abolished dyarchy at the Provincial level and introduced it at the Centre. There were two categories of federal subjects, reserved subjects and Transferred subjects.

Bicameral legislature: Under the Government of India Act, 1935, the Central Legislature was bicameral, consisting of Federal Assembly and Council of States. The Council of States was to be upper house and a permanent body with one third of its membership retiring every 3rd year. The Federal Assembly was the lower house with the tenure of five years.
Retention of Communal Electorate: Separate electorates were provided for Muslims, Sikhs and others, but not to Depressed Classes.

Abolition of India Council: The new Act abolished India Council and provided for the appointment by the Secretary of State and his team of Advisers whose number was not to be less than 3 and not more than 65.
Federal Court: The Government of India Act, 1935 provided for the establishment of a Federal Court which would interpret the Act and adjudicate disputes relating to the federal matters.

The Government of India Act 1919 made a provision for a review committee on its working after 10 years.

Thus, the Indian statutory commission popularly known as the Simon commission was appointed in 1927.
A commission established by Baldwin to inquire into political conditions in British India.

It met a hostile reception in India, and was boycotted there because it had no Indian members.
